then.text: Keep filling that Timeline, {player}. History's a relay race, and you're holding the baton now. Mind you don't drop it in the Irwell.
You cracked a cipher in Hut 8 and stood next to Colossus? Tommy Flowers paid for some of its parts himself, you know, and then had to keep quiet about it for thirty years.
And it all started a few streets from here, with the Baby. Now you know how a computer thinks: ones and noughts, very fast, built by people.
Take these, with my thanks. And keep at the Timeline: it runs from the Iron Bridge to AlphaFold, and every era you fill in earns you a gadget.

else.text: You've seen Colossus, lovely. Now the cipher: the codebreaker in Hut 8 has a practice message for you.
Bletchley Park next: head east out of Oxford. Crack a practice cipher in Hut 8, then find Colossus in Block H. Come back and tell me everything.

then.text: You've read about the Baby. Now count like it. Every number it held was a row of dots, each one on or off.
Ones and noughts, all the way down. That's every photo, song and text message you've ever had.
Now Bletchley Park, east out of Oxford. Crack a practice cipher in Hut 8, find Colossus in Block H, then come back to me.

else.text: Read the plaque about the Baby first. It's just there, by the path.
Dr Bethan Howells, retired physics teacher, Aberystwyth born and bred. I'm making a Timeline of Invention, and my knees have retired too, so I need a pair of legs.
Nearly eighty years ago, at the university down the road, a machine called the Baby ran the first program ever stored in a computer's own memory. Your phone is its great-great-grandchild.
Read the plaque about it, just there, then come back and I'll show you how it counted. After that: Bletchley Park.
Every plaque about an invention, every machine you see, goes on your Timeline. It's in the Almanac. Fill in an era and you get a little gadget for your trouble.

then.text: Do come in! Welcome to the Heritage Experience. Free tote bag with every signature.
No, you've had yours. We keep a list. It is a long and friendly list.

else.text: Ah! A member of the public! Splendid. Do come in. Mind the bunting, it is ethically sourced.
Ambrose Vane, Chairman of the Enclosure. Welcome to the Manchester Heritage Experience.
Our mission is simple. Britain's old places are under-curated. A stone circle is just a circle with no signage.
So we shall look after them. Properly. With turnstiles.
And the old legends, the sleepy ones under the hills? We shall bind them, tag them and put them somewhere safe. Somewhere ours.
{rival} pops up from behind a table of merchandise, wearing three tote bags and a lanyard.
{player}! Look at this! Free tote bag! Free water bottle! Free pen that is also a torch!
They said I can stream the launch if I tag them. That's free reach, {player}. Free!
Quite. Everyone benefits. Especially the people who own the pen factory.
He's a bit smug, isn't he. But the pen is genuinely a torch.

rail_guard.text: Piccadilly Station. Where do you fancy going?

warden_pop.text: We are not fencing anything. We are curating access.
The canal towpath is closed for heritage enhancement. The enhancement is the fence.
The tote bags are excellent, by the way. Very sturdy.

then.text: Hi-vis. Excellent. You may stand near the tram line. Not on it.
Christmas markets in Albert Square. Mulled wine at eight quid a cup. You keep the cup, so that's alright then.
Leaves on the line. Every autumn. You'd think a tram would have got used to trees by now.
Points freeze, trams stop, everyone tuts. Tutting's practically a Manchester sport.
Proper Manchester rain this. The trams love it. Shiny rails, shiny me.
Fog on the tracks. You hear the tram bell before you see the tram. Lovely, that.
First tram of the day! I've got my flask. Some traditions never die.

tram_fan.text: {greeting} Manchester's Metrolink opened in 1992. I was there. I had a flask.
It was the first modern tram system in the country. I know because I tell everybody.

then.text: Fog on the Rochdale Canal. Go slow and shout 'boat' a lot, that's my method.

boater.text: This is the Rochdale Canal. Opened 1804, closed in the 1950s, reopened in 2002. Nine lives, like a cat.
The Bridgewater Canal, round the corner, is often called the first canal of the Industrial Revolution. Opened in 1761 to carry coal.

student.text: Rutherford split the atom here in 1917. And the first stored-program computer ran here in 1948. They called it the Baby.
The Baby weighed about a tonne. Teething problems, you could say.

then.text: Is that a bucket hat? Respect. Nineteen ninety-one called, and it wants its vibe back.
Taking Halloween requests. So far it's been Thriller eleven times and 'go away' once.
Penny for the Guy? Card's fine, love.
Tap it on the hat. Contactless Guys are the future.
Christmas set: three carols, a bit of Wham! and far too much Slade. Folk get generous in December.
Raining, is it? Perfect. My rain song's got real atmosphere today.
Sunshine in Manchester! I don't have a song for this. I'll have to make one up.
Evening crowd's coming out. They tip better when the street lights come on.

busker.text: {greeting} Any requests? I know nine chords and a song about the rain.
Everyone asks for the one about the rain.

then.text: Welcome to the tour! Yes, it's raining. It's Manchester. The rain is part of the tour.
A sunny tour! Quick, everyone look at the Town Hall before it clouds over.

town_hall_guide.text: The Town Hall opened in 1877. Gothic revival, big clock, bigger bees.
The worker bee is Manchester's emblem. It stands for hard work. The city did not invent the bee, but it did perfect the queue.

then.text: Even the bees carry brollies in Manchester. Well, the painted ones would if they could.
Hold onto your hat, it's blowing a gale down Deansgate. The bees are staying grounded.

bee_fan.text: Spot the bees on the lamp posts, the pavements, the bins. They're everywhere.
The worker bee has been the city's symbol since the Victorians. Busy city, busy bees, busy brolly.

manchester_night_nurse.text: Off to the Royal Infirmary for the night shift. Twelve hours, three cups of tea, one biscuit if I'm lucky.
Manchester's lovely at night. Quiet streets, wet pavements, the odd fox having a nosy.
Get yourself home and get some sleep, love. That's my professional opinion.

manchester_fox_watcher.text: Shh. There's a vixen by the bins on the corner. She comes past every night about now.
City foxes are cleverer than country ones. They know the takeaway closing times.
Red torch, see? It doesn't scare them. A white one does, and so does shouting.

isles_kasia.text: {greeting} Dzień dobry! That's good day, in Polish. Say JEN DOH-bri. Close enough and you get a pączek.

My great-grandad flew Hurricanes with 303 Squadron in the Battle of Britain: Poles flying for Britain after they'd lost their own country. After the war many couldn't go home to a Poland under Soviet control, so they stayed. Parliament passed a law to resettle them, in 1947.
Then in 2004 Poland joined the EU and lots more of us came, me included. Polish is the second most spoken language in England now. Pierogi next to pasties. Everybody wins.
